Diefenbaker (Prince Albert): Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity arising from a request made by the Clerk of the Privy Council, Mr. Peter Michael Pitfield, on behalf of the cabinet for a legal opinion from the law officers of the Crown on the question as to how the name of the capital city of Canada could be changed from Ottawa to the National Capital Region. In reply, the deputy attorney general stated that it could be done by cabinet issuing an order in council advising the Governor General to issue a proclamation to change the name of the seat of government to National Capital Region, whereupon the Governor General would issue the required proclamation in the name of the Queen under the Great Seal of Canada. Such proclamation, according to the advice given, would issue from the Governor General as representative of the Queen and not from the Queen personally. It was added, however, that it should issue in her name, as the Queen is referred to specifically in section 16 of the British North America Act, which provides that:
Until the Queen otherwise directs the Seat of the Government of Canada shall be Ottawa.
The fact that the legal opinion has been asked for as to whether action could be taken without parliament's approval reveals that the government is considering changing the name of the capital, a course that Canadians everywhere will resent, and furthermore reveals a flagrant contempt of parliament.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF AMBASSADOR TO CHILE TO PROTEST INHUMAN TREATMENT OF CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not given any consideration to the possibility suggested by the hon. member, but Canada has made its position very clear on the question of human rights in Chile. We have made our position known on several occasions and in several ways, both directly to the government of Chile and at the United Nations. We have urged that human rights be respected in that country in accordance with the universal declaration on human rights, so there is no equivocation with respect to the position of the Government of Canada.
However, I believe our concern with respect to human rights in Chile has taken a much more concrete form than the expressions I mentioned. Since the coup d'etat, Canada has played and continues to play a leading role in the resettlement of people from that country occasioned by the change in regime, and so far nearly 4,000 people have been authorized to come to Canada under our special immigration program. I believe that that is an extremely important aspect of our treatment of the question of human rights in Chile and ought to be borne in mind and related to the consequences which might occur to that important humanitarian program if we took action such as suggested by the hon. gentleman.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the long-awaited study of the accounts of Canada tabled by the President of the Treasury Board. It was in May, 1973, that the Treasury Board secretariat first announced its intention to critically examine the concepts underlying the financial information system of the government through an interdepartmental steering committee. For many years the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, and the Auditor General, in their respective reports have questioned certain financial practices as being inconsistent with the stated principles on which the government's accounts are kept.
It is refreshing, therefore, to see the initiative taken by Treasury Board, in response to the committee and the Auditor General, to examine "the purposes, principles and practices which should govern the form of the accounts of Canada" and to present constructive proposals for parliament's consideration so that the accounts of Canada reflect a fair, complete and accurate record of the Government of Canada's finances. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, as parliamentarians and as users of the accounts of Canada, we welcome this report if the proposals presented help us in our daily task to examine more meaningfully government expenditures and, indeed, help us to strengthen parliament's control over the public purse.
We welcome the referral of this study to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and will be pleased to report back to this House in due course on our deliberations.

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the House that nuclear co-operation agreements have been signed with the governments of the Republic of Korea and the Republic or Argentina. I am tabling copies of the texts of these agreements. I should also like to table the background paper on nuclear safeguards and Canadian safeguards policy which may be of interest to hon. members, and also extracts from a document published by the International Atomic Energy Agency which outlines the safeguards procedures and inspection systems in place by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
The agreement with the Republic of Korea was signed, as I mentioned yesterday, at Seoul on January 26. I will allow the sale to the Republic of Korea of a CANDU power reactor produced by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to go forward. The attendant commercial and financial arrangements have already been concluded. The Republic of Korea, as hon. members are aware, is a developing country which is in the process of significant industrialization.
The economy of the Republic of Korea is basically sound. Its pattern of growth has been remarkable in recent years, but it has large power requirements over the coming periods which its indigenous fuel resources are not in a position to satisfy. As part of its efforts to generate sufficient energy for its programs of industrialization and development, the Republic of Korea has established a significant program of nuclear power generation. The acquisition of a CANDU power reactor is intended to supplement the country's nuclear power generation program. The Republic of Korea is already building a power reactor supplied from the United States and is contracting for one additional unit from that source.
The agreement with Argentina was signed in Buenos Aires today. It covers the sale of a CANDU reactor to the Argentine Republic and attendant technical co-operation pursuant to contracts which were concluded in 1974. Worldwide inflation since that time has created difficulties and the commercial terms of those latter contracts are currently being renegotiated.
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements
Argentina is an important Latin-American country which has had harmonious relations with its neighbours for over 100 years. It is a member of the International Atomic Energy Agency. It has had a successful nuclear development program for over 25 years and operates a number of reserach reactors as well as a heavy water moderated power reactor built with the co-operation of the Federal Republic of Germany.
The co-operation to be undertaken under these two agreements reflects the position announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1975 when he noted that Canada would continue to seek to make available to developing countries the benefits of the peaceful applications of nuclear energy, provided that adequate guarantees against the possible diversion of such co-operation to non-peaceful, explosive purposes were available. This is a position endorsed by other nuclear suppliers.
These agreements provide that identified nuclear exports, including nuclear technology in physical form, shall only be authorized on the basis of coverage by an intergovernmental guarantee: First, that the items supplied or items produced with these, including subsequent generations, will not be diverted to any non-peaceful or explosive purpose; second, that these guarantees are verified through inspection mechanisms of the International Atomic Energy Agency; third, that the retransfer of items supplied and items produced with these including subsequent generations of nuclear material only be done with the consent of the Government of Canada; fourth, that the enrichment and reprocessing of nuclear material supplied, or nuclear material produced with times supplied, only be done with the consent of the government of Canada; fifth, that IAEA safeguards and other mechanisms of bilateral verification for aspects of guarantees, where the IAEA system is not applicable, be in place for the life of the supplied item or for items susceptible to these guarantees produced from these items; and sixth, that adequate measures for the physical security of materials be in place to protect the supplied items from the threat of subnational diversion.
The safeguards commitments, including the application of the International Atomic Energy Agency inspection system, undertaken by the Republic of Korea and the Republic of Argentina represent juridical assurances of a high order which fully meet international standards and Canadian safeguards policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is whether these agreements for the sale of nuclear reactors and arrangements regarding nuclear co-operation are adequate. Our experience with India has shown the danger that technology can be used to develop techniques for the making of nuclear explosions or which have the potential at least for atomic or nuclear bombs. In view of the Indian experience, we in Canada, and the Government of Canada, have a special responsibility regarding the sale of nuclear reactors. I recognize the potential for contradiction inherent in the concept of nonproliferation, that is, that everybody will agree not to proliferate the use of nuclear bombs, and this sort of thing, and that in compensation the benefits of nuclear knowledge will be shared generally. I recognize the potential

January 30, 1976
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements
contradiction involved, therefore, in imposing severe limits upon the sale of nuclear reactors.
I recognize, also, the importance of sharing the benefits and the risks of a growing tendency to reject the concept of non-proliferation if countries without other sources of electricity and power are denied the benefits of this kind of reactor. But the risks of illicit proliferation such as, I am afraid, took place in India are so great, and the process of illicit proliferation constitutes such a menace to world peace, that I believe it is far better for us to take some time to get in place solid international safeguards for peace. Certainly, it is not good enough to claim that we are imposing the highest standard of safeguards in the world, if that should happen to be true, because the question with regard to either or both of these sales is: Does this sale by us constitute a serious risk in the total context, which includes what other countries are now doing or may be doing with the regard to the sale of plutonium recycling plants, for example? We must look at the total context.
It is said that France is prepared to sell a plutonium recycling plant. The minister made no reference to this in his statement about Korea, nor in connection with the Argentinian situation did he make any reference to the report that West Germany is prepared to make a very large package deal with Brazil. The assumption among many people is that this may lead to nuclear rivalry between Brazil and Argentina. This is part of the context in which Canada is entering into these agreements with Korea and Argentina.
There is only one reason why today a country like Korea, or any modest country, would want a recycling plant, and that is to develop fissionable material suitable for the development of bombs-because it is not economical in terms of the development of electrical power. So we can talk about our humanitarian desires, our desire to help Korea in peaceful development, and the same with Argentina, but is this so much our motivation in making these sales as our desire to make the sales?

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
It is important that we have very strict agreements and a very strict understanding among all countries which are capable of exporting reactors or nuclear technology. I hope Canada and the other countries involved, of which there are only a relatively small number, develop such a strict agreement. It is now reported that some kind of agreement will be reached but it will be far from strict. I believe Canada should have been prepared to wait and to ask for a general moratorium, to set an example by demanding adequate safeguards to be provided by all the countries capable of exporting reactors or nuclear technology. I suggest this particularly in view of the unstable situation that exists in the part of Asia where Korea is located, and certainly the unstable conditions that exist within Argentina.
When you look at these agreements and safeguards that are negotiated, what do you find? I have not had an opportunity to examine them fully, because the minister sent us copies of these agreements only today at 10.30 a.m. I know he has a very high view of my intelligence, but my

intelligence is not such as to allow me to analyse these complicated documents within that period of time. But it is a matter of such importance that I would suggest to the hon. gentleman, old parliamentarian that he is, that even from his government vantage point he could not regard this as a satisfactory method of discussing an arrangement of such vital importance to the world.
In the United States the government has to go to Congress before a deal is completed so that Congress has an opportunity to raise objections. That is the minimum which this government should be prepared to provide for this parliament. The way we are now proceeding is most unsatisfactory. In matters relating to something as basically important to this country and to the world as the sale of a nuclear reactor and the possible consequences of that sale, this government should be prepared to table in the House the agreement it proposes to make and give parliament a reasonable opportunity to study the proposals and to raise objections, at the very least.
Much of the technology that has been made available to Korea and to Argentina can be applied to non-peaceful purposes. We have no assurances and no indications that the sanctions will be adequate. What could Canada do if Argentina or Korea failed to live up to these obligations? The minister said there would be inspections under international arrangements. I have no reason to believe, from anything I knew before or from anything the minister has said today, that the quality and degree of inspection that can be provided by an international agency is at all adequate to prevent unfortunate consequences from developing. Certainly, the minister could not give us any assurances today. I have no reason to believe that international inspection arrangements are adequate today, or that the international agents will in fact be in a position to inspect all the aspects that are necessary.
I do not want to take too much time, but I do not apologize for the time I am taking because these matters are very important. I say that Canada's inspection and control in these two situations seems to be very limited. I say that the context as a whole is dangerous. I say that our government should be prepared to wait and to push for really adequate international arrangements before rushing into these sales. Also, I say it is unfortunate that so many exporting countries which have the technology are taking a commercial approach to the sale of nuclear reactors and nuclear technology. I am sorry to see my own country seeming to give such weight to the commercial aspects of these arrangements.

I do not ask the minister what the terms of the deal are with regard to financing and this sort of thing. It is too late to stop this. But I hope the government will give us an undertaking that there will be no further completed transactions of this sort until such transaction is tabled in the House, as is the case in our neighbouring country. I ask that we not be presented with a fait accompli; that we be given an opportunity to study what is being proposed-and, who knows, we might even be able to bring something to the attention of this government which could be useful to it.
January 30, 1976

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many thousands of Canadians will be saddened today by the announcement the minister has just made, especially coming from a minister for whom many Canadians have deep respect. When he was appointed to this high office many of us hoped he would pursue a foreign policy for Canada which would not be dominated by commercial considerations. The minister said in the statement he made a few moments ago that the signing of these agreements with Argentina and South Korea was in line with the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1975, to the effect that Canada would continue to make available to developing countries the benefits of nuclear energy, provided there were adequate guarantees against the possible diversion of such facilities to nonpeaceful or explosive purposes.
Therefore, the whole question arises as to whether it is possible to have adequate guarantees and adequate safeguards. Just a few days ago an American nuclear scientist visiting Canada said there can be no adequate safeguards and that the only wise course to follow is to reduce the sale of nuclear reactors wherever the political situation is unstable and unpredictable. Certainly, the two countries with whom the government has just signed an agreement would come into the class of being both unstable and unpredictable.
The minister is placing his entire faith in the periodic inspections which will be made by the International Atomic Energy Agency, commonly known as IAEA. This organization has neither the power of enforcement nor the adequately trained staff to ensure adequate safeguards. The last report shows that the IAEA has 135 employees of whom less than 70 are nuclear scientists. In 1974 there were 562 nuclear plants in 33 countries, in 1975 there were 650 nuclear plants in 38 countries, and it is anticipated the figure will be well over 1,000 by 1980. How do less than 70 nuclear scientists possibly hope to carry on adequate inspection services in a situation like that?
The IAEA is doing its best; there is no doubt about that. They recently reported, however, that only 95 per cent of the plutonium extracted from the radium waste of reactors could be accounted for with accuracy. They hope, they say, in a number of years to get this up to 99 per cent. That may sound very comforting to some people, but let us consider the situation. It is estimated that in 1975 there were 17,000 pounds of plutonium produced. Now, 5 per cent of that is 850 pounds, from which could be made 55 nuclear bombs. Even when we get to 99 per cent of a certainty with respect to accounting for plutonium, that still leaves 170 pounds, which is enough to make 10 or 11 nuclear bombs.
The danger is not just the possibility of a nuclear war. One of the real dangers is that terrorist groups may get their hands on quantities of plutonium. Neither South Korea nor Argentina, in my opinion, can be considered stable in the present world situation. No one who was at the discussion at the United Nations a few months ago when the whole question of North Korea and South Korea was before the United Nations General Assembly would think for a moment, with the gathering troop concentrations on the border, that the possibility of an outbreak of war is extremely remote. It certainly is not. There could be
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements war on that peninsula at almost any time. Argentina has had political instability for some time and there is a distinct possibility that the government there might be overthrown. What kind of government will take its place, a government for whom we have made it possible to produce plutonium and to make nuclear weapons?
The danger does not really lie in the nuclear reactor. The danger lies in the toxic waste from the reactor from which plutonium can be extracted. The only way to extract it is with an extraction plant or reprocessing plant, and both South Korea and Argentina have purchased reprocessing plants. It is significant that the United States and the United Kingdom have both refused to sell reprocessing plants to these countries, but they have been able to secure them from France.
When the minister was going to Korea some months ago, we asked him if he would ascertain from the President of South Korea why that country had obtained a reprocessing plant. When the minister came back he told us in the House that the President had assured him that the reprocessing plant was for scientific research. How naive can the minister be? The only possible purpose in having a reprocessing plant is to extract plutonium, and the only possible use for a toxic commodity like plutonium is to make bombs. Yet both of these countries have reprocessing plants, and we are selling them nuclear reactors. They already have other nuclear reactors but they are now going to get a CANDU reactor by virtue of this agreement.
I submit to the minister and to the House that there is a heavy burden upon the people of Canada with respect to what we are doing at this time. A little over 30 years ago, when the first atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, the world was shocked and conscience-stricken about the new and terrible powers which were placed in the hands of mankind. If at that time the nations of the world had been able to restrict the spread of nuclear weapons, we might be able to sleep more easily. Instead, the nuclear club has spread at an alarming rate. An anthropologist visiting Canada just a few days ago said that, considering the pollution of the air, water and earth, and considering the proliferation of nuclear weapons, he could not see the survival of the human race beyond the year 2000. The fact is that the world is living on the edge of Armageddon. It may be that the contribution we have made to that situation up until now has been done unknowingly, but the step now being taken by the government is being taken deliberately and the government has a very heavy burden on its conscience.
The Canadian people will have to ask themselves whether they want to continue contributing to the possibility of a nuclear holocaust. Certainly, future generations will hold those of us who sit in this parliament responsible if we are plunged into a nuclear war ourselves, or any part of the world in the years which lie ahead.
In closing, I want to renew the plea I made to the minister yesterday. I have not changed my mind as a result of hearing the statement of the minister today. I do not think it is enough for a crucial decision like this to be made by the government and then members of parliament to be given a five-minute statement by the minister, two or three minutes of reply from each of the political parties, and that is all.

January 30, 1976
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
I agree wholeheartedly with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who says that an international agreement of this importance ought to be submitted to parliament before it is signed. I know that traditionally the executive has always taken the position that it has the right to sign any international agreement, and then parliament at some time or other can move a motion of no confidence; but I refer the hon. gentleman to one of the patron saints of the Liberal party, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, who was prime minister of Canada, I think, longer than any other person in the history of this nation. On April 12, 1928, this is what he said in parliament:
I submit that the day has passed when any government or executive should feel that they should take it upon themselves without the approval of parliament, to commit a country to obligations involving any considerable financial outlays or active undertakings. In all cases where obligations of such a character are being assumed internationally, parliament itself should be assured of having the full right of approving what is done before binding commitments are made. I would not confine parliamentary approval only to those matters which involve military sanctions and the like. I feel parliamentary approval should apply where there are involved matters of large expenditure or political considerations of a far-reaching character.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the government that there can be no international commitment of more far-reaching character than the signing of these two agreements with South Korea and Argentina and selling them a CANDU reactor. Both nations have in their possession reprocessing plants from which they can extract plutonium. The minister shakes his head, but I would be glad to hear from him about that in the question period.
I submit since the government has already signed the agreements, the very least the minister can do is to say that he will introduce a motion in the House asking the House to approve these two agreements. Members of parliament would then have an opportunity to express their opinion on the matter, and the government would have some idea of public reaction and could govern itself accordingly in the future. I hope that if there are any other agreements of this character-I trust there will not be-the government will submit the matter to parliament prior to signing them.

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF NUCLEAR CO-OPERATION AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard the minister's statement on the two agreements signed with South Korea and Argentina concerning the sale of CANDU reactors. I am sure the minister was aware of the responsibilities he was taking in signing these agreements. I believe he has taken every precaution to make sure that these two countries merely want to take advantage of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.
In his statement, the minister said that the Korean economy is basically sound and that its growth rate has been outstanding those last years. But its future needs for energy will be enormous and will not be satisfied by its own oil resources. We must always face facts. When a country which wants to develop itself and surge ahead has no other course than to ask for external aid, as Korea has asked Canada, I think it is reasonable to take all the

necessary precautions. A few moments ago I have heard the leader of the opposition say that the emphasis was on the commerical aspect. In my opinion, we are perhaps taking the commercial aspect into account, as in any market consideration, but I think we must not forget the social aspect. We must not consider only the matter of explosives.
A few moments ago, an NDP speaker was mentioning the atomic danger. But the danger represented by atomic bombs exists across this country, Mr. Speaker, since Canada is full of nuclear devices.
There is still about the fear of atomic bombs. All major countries have the atomic bomb. If some countries want to use that modern energy, that energy by excellence which is atomic energy for pacific purposes, provided all possible precautions are taken, I think Canada is welcome to help those countries. As long as they stay within the pacific action they want to implant in their countries, well, modern explosive means have to be used for pacific purposes if the necessary safeguards are there.
I think the minister took the necessary precautions. Accidents might happen. The minister himself might have surprises. But who says who is going to govern tomorrow? In any country, even Canada, who says who is going to govern us tomorrow? I would not wish that we be governed even by the NDP tomorrow. But one cannot judge the good intentions of this government on future assumptions. I simply say that precautions were taken.
It is good trade business, of course, let us not hide that fact; it is a good thing for Canada to be dealing with those countries at the trade level to open other doors for us. If it does not, other countries will, others are ready to do so. I noted earlier that the United States have already begun building a nuclear reactor bought in the United States for Korea. I think Canada is no worse than others as long as we stay within the bounds of pacifism simply to bring a country more in line with modern methods and it is beneficial at the same time for our country because of trade balances. I think we must not close the doors but extent our trade possibilities to other countries, contrary to the practice of past years where we always limited ourselves to dealing with two or three countries. We always had a trade deficit. Naturally, the subject is touchy; we are talking about atomic energy, but if that energy is used properly as set forth in the agreements now signed between the minister and the countries involved it will bring only positive results.
