speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. We shall now proceed to a question period in which hon. members will question the Secretary of State for External Affairs on his statement. Unfortunately, the minister is not here, which puts the House in a difficult position. If hon. members do not mind, we shall wait for a few minutes until the minister arrives.
Agreed.
Here is the minister.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs relating to the assistance for Korea but not directly relating to the safeguards agreement? Can the minister inform the House, in general terms, of the financial arrangements for the transaction with Korea, approximately how much credit is being advanced by Canada to the Republic of Korea, the duration of the proposed loan and the rate of interest?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall do my best to supply some of the details asked for by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to the financing of the reactor for the Republic of Korea. The total cost of the reactor is approximately $500 million, and I understand that Canadian government financing is in the amount of $300 million. I have no details beyond that except that the amount is repayable in 30 semi-annual instalments commencing not later than six months after commissioning, or October, 1982, whichever comes first. Interest terms are not generally made public because of the effect such information might have on future negotiating positions in other transactions. That is all the information I have on the financing aspect of the Republic of Korea's undertaking.

Mr. Speaker, am I to understand from the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the people of this country will not be able to form an assessment of the prudence of the financial aspects of this deal because of some alleged effect upon our competitive position? What possible justification is there for refusing to disclose to members of this House the rate of interest so that the people of Canada can know to what extent, if any, they are subsidizing this transaction?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have given the justification for not disclosing the information. Frankly, I do not have the information at hand at the moment. I inquired about it, but the practice is not to reveal the terms of loans, for the reason given. I suggest that the Leader of the Opposition may follow the matter up with my colleague who is responsible, basically, for the financing aspects of the arrangement.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to accept the minister's suggestion and will do as he suggests, because I do not think secrecy would be acceptable either to parliament or to the people of Canada. Does the Secretary of State for External Affairs share my view that the situation-that is, the situation regarding the sale of nuclear reactors, nuclear technology and related matters-is going
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements from bad to worse in the sense that West Germany has offered a big package to Brazil, and France seems to be prepared to sell recycling plants for the recovery of plutonium to various countries?
If the minister shares my concern in this regard, why was the Government of Canada not prepared to wait a bit before completing this transaction so that it could bring all possible pressure to bear on the five or six other countries, including Britain, West Germany, France, the United States and one or two others, to agree mutually on practices and safeguards which would result in a reasonable sharing of the benefits of nuclear technology and, at the same time, safeguard the world from the danger of a nuclear holocaust?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the concern of the Leader of the Opposition and the concern expressed by others who spoke earlier today. I assure the hon. member that the question of non-proliferation was a dominant consideration in the negotiations preceding the signing of these agreements. Certainly, I paid dominant and paramount attention to the safeguards aspects of these agreements, in the interests of non-proliferation.
The Leader of the Opposition asked why we would not consider a moratorium. We concluded that it would not be useful if Canada withheld its sale of these reactors at this stage in the expectation that this would bring pressure to bear on other suppliers, as it would not be a good course of action. Probably it would result in Canada's losing sales to other nuclear suppliers, and we would also lose whatever influence we are exercising-and I believe it is considerable-with other suppliers in upgrading the general level of international safeguards. That is why we do not agree with his proposal for a moratorium. We believe it would not have any visible, obvious effect in this situation. It might even have a negative effect.
The Leader of the Opposition talked about reprocessing plants. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands spoke of both the Republic of Korea and the Republic of Argentina as being in possession of reprocessing plants. That is not true, and I am gratified to be able to tell the House that in the course of negotiations with the Republic of Korea the government of that country advised us it had cancelled its order for a reprocessing plant from France. So it has no way in which to complete the fuel cycle. Likewise, there is no reprocessing plant of military or commercial significance in existence in Argentina. There is, as I understand it, a small laboratory model of a reprocessing plant.
When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands conjures up visions of all these pounds of plutonium, I can tell him they are not to be found either in the Republic of Korea or in Argentina. These large amounts are to be found in the industrialized countries of the world. I do not share his view, or that of other hon. members, that we ought to deny to the developing countries of the world an opportunity to share in this new technology.

Hear, hear!

January 30,1976
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think we ought to conduct a debate on the level of fact, and what I have just said represents the fact with respect to processing plants.

Before putting some questions to the minister, I wonder whether I might, for his own protection, draw attention to the text of his statement this morning? On page four, in the fourth line or so-he might check it in Hansard-he spoke of "co-operation for non-peaceful explosive purposes". I feel sure he must have meant "non-peaceful or explosive purposes".
As to the statement the minister has just made, let me say this: when I commented this morning to the effect that both Argentina and South Korea either possessed or were in the process of possessing reprocessing plants, I noticed that the minister was shaking his head. Now he tells us definitely that they do not have reprocessing plants. Well, Mr. Speaker, a report from London by Peter Calamai at the time of the International Energy Conference last summer definitely stated that the information coming out of that conference was to the effect that Argentina had obtained a reprocessing plant from France, and that South Korea was in the process of obtaining one, also from France. The minister says today that Korea has cancelled the order. May I ask him now whether there is any provision in the agreement that in the event of South Korea changing its mind and securing a reprocessing plant, the agreement will automatically be suspended?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, that is not in the agreement. What is in the agreement-and it is a main provision-is that Canada is entitled to a hold on the reprocessing of any spent fuel, and we have indicated to the Republic of Korea that we would not at the present time be prepared to give consent for the reprocessing of any such spent fuel. Of course, that requirement within the agreement is to some extent inoperative because of the decision taken by Korea to cancel its order for a reprocessing plant from France. We think that is a positive element in the situation. I am satisfied, also, that the United States shares our view that nuclear technology ought to be made available to developing countries such as the Republic of Korea for peaceful purposes only, and I am satisfied that the United States will work diligently to secure that objective also.

I do
not think the United States comes into the picture. The deal is between Canada and South Korea. The minister cannot give any assurance that South Korea, which was negotiating the purchase of a reprocessing plant, will not later obtain one. His answer, as I understand it, was that Canada would have control over any plutonium which may be produced from the waste material from the CANDU reactor. I should like to ask how that control will be exercised. Does Canada propose to repatriate the plutonium? In what way would control be exercised over the recycling of the waste?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is right in stating we have not required that the spent fuel be returned to Canada. We did consider that course seriously, but we abandoned it for two reasons: first, because of the environ-

mental implications for Canada and, second, because it would not add significantly to the non-proliferation objective we were seeking. The inspection system to be carried out by the International Atomic Energy Agency is intended to detect the diversion of materials to non-agreed purposes. That is the purpose of the inspection system, one which relies on instrumentation as well as on personnel. That is the way we look after the point the hon. gentleman has raised.

In
view of the fact that IAEA itself does not undertake to account for anything beyond 95 per cent of the plutonium extracted, it seems to me that the minister is leaning upon a very slender reed. Mr. Speaker, I have one final question. The minister's statement today, together with the discussion that has taken place, seems to underline the need for a much wider discussion with respect to this important subject. Hon. members generally may be satisfied that the alleged safeguards will guarantee the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, but I am not satisfied that the two countries to whom we are selling these reactors constitute stable and reliable areas but, rather, are countries to which we ought not to be sending nuclear plants which ultimately could be used for the production of nuclear bombs.
Is the minister now prepared to consider the suggestion I made in the House yesterday, that he himself introduce a motion in the House in order for the House to have an opportunity to discuss this matter fully? I cannot believe that the government considers this matter of so little importance that the few moments we have had to discuss it today are sufficient for dealing with such a far-reaching subject that could have serious consequences not only for ourselves but the whole of mankind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the importance that the hon. member attaches to this question, but I would remind him that we did discuss this question fully in parliament a few months ago, at which time the same arguments were put forward. We also had a very full discussion of the question in the standing committee on external affairs a month or so ago. The subject, in itself, has been very fully aired. However, I will consider the suggestion of the hon. member as to whether there is some way that further parliamentary examination could be made, not only of the agreements but also of the background material, which I think will prove useful for all of us in understanding the nature of the problem and what steps are being taken to apply safeguards. I will consider the hon. member's suggestion.

Mr. Speaker, was the question of the protection of the environment considered, and does this agreement cover the storage and disposal of nuclear waste materials from the environmental point of view, be it in Canada or in the countries gaining the nuclear reactors? Secondly, are these agreements similar to the agreement Canada is currently seeking with India subsequent to its nuclear explosion, in regard to Canadian aid to that country?
January 30, 1976

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the safety features of a nuclear reactor when it is in operation will, of course, be controlled by the host country and will be its responsibility. In Argentina, where already a power reactor supplied by Germany is in operation, and in Korea where one is under construction, supplied by the United States, the question of safety is basically a matter for their concern. To my knowledge, there is nothing in this agreement that would impose environmental regulations upon the recipient country. We are presently in negotiation with India in regard to safeguards for the uncompleted reactor there, but these negotiations have not yet been completed. Obviously, the negotiations are directed toward increasing the safeguards for that particular project.

Mr. Speaker, may I put a supplementary to each of my two questions? Is the minister saying that when Canada exports a reactor it feels no obligation in regard to the fact that the reactor will add to the world pollution problem? We share a responsibility for the disposal of nuclear waste from that reactor. At least we have a responsibility to see that it will be adequately handled. Does the minister know the method that will be used to handle this waste disposal, or is it to be handled by the country concerned? This is of major concern to the world. Just as we are calling for a moratorium on the profilera-tion aspects, there should be a similar moratorium regarding environmental control. Would the minister not agree with that statement?
My second supplementary question is this: Does the minister really expect any success with his negociations with India, in view of the fact that India has now started an external aid program greater than the $100 million with which we provide India by way of foreign aid? Bear in mind that $100 million is a small amount relative to a $2.5 billion expenditure. Is there any hope for the sanctions? This relates to the broader question of whether there is any real sanction at all, once we have allowed reactors to leave Canada, so far as controlling them is concerned. What sanctions are available other than foreign aid which has proven ineffective?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have suspended our nuclear co-operation with India. That was a painful choice for Canada as well as for India. Because of our mutual desire to get out of the situation created by that painful cessation of nuclear co-operation we are now negotiating with India. Although we have not yet succeeded, we are still working on it. I have issued instructions to our negotiating team to resume negotiations in Indian in the month of February, and we will then know whether we will succeed. If we fail, the government will then be faced with a very serious situation. But I hope we will not fail.

Mr. Speaker, would the minister advise the House whether there was an attempt in our negotiations with South Korea to put in the contract a force majeure provision so that, in the event that there was a violation of any of the commitments that have been given in these matters either by Argentina or South Korea, the Government of Canada would have the power, at least legally, to go into those countries and remove any of the fissionable material that may have been stored there, or remove any of the equipment that had been sold? Was there any attempt
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements to have such a clause provided in the contract and, if so, what was the the reaction of South Korea, and why did it not accept such provision?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a provision in the contract or agreement-I would have to look at it again-providing for the return of any material, including the reactor, in the event of any violations. But there are practical obstacles in the way of the execution of such an agreement which would be even more difficult in the situation described by the hon. member.

We should have something like a conditional sales agreement. There have been recent reports that nuclear exporting countries have been meeting in order to rationalize their sales procedure and introduce additional international standards regarding safeguards. In other words, there were reports, though not official, that Canada and other countries were participating with countries like France, West Germany, and so on, with regard to rationalizing the sales approach so that we do not have people bargaining off the safeguards in order to make a sale in the face of other competitors. Would the minister advise the House whether such meetings took place, and also whether any general agreement was arrived at in terms of international safeguard provisions governing sales by nuclear exporting countries to various purchasers?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there have been meetings among suppliers, including Canada, and one objective of this series of meetings was to upgrade the standard of safeguards among the supplying countries as one effective method of improving prospects for non-proliferation. We have put forward proposals at those meetings and I am certain we are in the vanguard of those who advocate improved and upgraded safeguards. Some progress has been made, and I hope that when the process is completed I will be able to report separately to the House on the results of these meetings of the nuclear suppliers. That is the primary way to achieve our objectives.

Can the minister advise why he did not consider delaying these sales until at least such time as those negotiations with other nuclear exporting countries were completed, on the simple basis that if the standards are higher than the ones we are now obtaining from Argentina and North Korea, we will have sold these nuclear reactors abroad at a lower standard than other nuclear exporting countries, therefore having a more immoral position, if I can put it that way, in terms of the way we flog these things abroad.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not fear that we will be placed in an immoral position as a result of any developments at a meeting of the nuclear suppliers. We have not declared the moratorium because we believe such a gesture would be futile and we would lose any influence we might have among the suppliers. In the meantime, the sales would be picked up by others and our position as a supplier in the way of influencing other suppliers would be, if not fatally damaged, at least seriously damaged.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote just one sentence of a speech the Prime Minister made to the

January 30, 1976
Nuclear Co-operation Agreements annual meeting of the Canadian Nuclear Association on June 17, 1975, because, I think it is important in this examination. The Prime Minister said:
Nuclear activity is one of the many ways in which man is now engaged which, if not made susceptible to reason and discipline, could become ultra-hazardous, even cataclysmic.
The Prime Minister went on to talk of our joint wisdom. I wonder if, within the minister's position, the use of the pronoun "our" in that case by the Prime Minister was a sort of royal or editorial "we", and that this parliament is not to have an opportunity to debate the agreements. If the Prime Minister is to be believed-and in these times that is very important-then surely he should be careful with his language. This is the place where joint wisdom might just perchance assist the government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that this is the place to share and to exchange views. I hope the material that I have made available, and the agreements themselves, will make it possible for hon. members to consider whether there are additional ways in which we can achieve the objective of non-proliferation.
I heard one extreme suggestion this afternoon, namely, that we declare a moratorium on the supply of these nuclear reactors which are urgently needed for power generation purposes and for social and economic development. I have heard that point of view, which I reject. I have heard very few suggestions, apart from the work that we ought to be doing in the suppliers' meetings, for the improvement of the international safeguards system that we have put into these two agreements.
I remind hon. members that we have taken every possible precaution in the case of the Republic of Korea and in the case of the Republic of Argentina so that no Canadian-supplied material, technology or equipment can be diverted for explosive purposes. That is our obligation. In the case of the Republic of Korea, we have been advised that their order for a reprocessing plant from France has been cancelled, thereby denying the opportunity at this stage of completing the fuel cycle.
At this stage.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I made a reply to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that I think is a response to the valid interjection of the Leader of the Opposition. However, we must also bear in mind that in the Republic of Korea at the present time there is under construction a power reactor supplied by the United States and a second one under order. The United States obviously has an interest and an obligation in this situation as well as Canada. In the case of the Republic of Argentina, there is no implication, direct or indirect, that Canada through its nuclear reactor is in any way adding to the freedom or ability of the Republic of Korea to develop nuclear weapons if it so decided.
Argentina, you mean.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Argentina does not have a reprocessing plant. The reactor that is there, supplied by Germany, is under safeguards. The heavy water that is supplied by the United States is also safeguarded. Canada is adding nothing to the infrastructure of the Republic of Argentina that

would justify the fears that have been raised by hon. members today. On the contrary, it has fully safeguarded its own participation. I believe it has created an incentive, if not an obligation, to possibly upgrade other suppliers operating at present or in the future, in the Republic of Argentina. I believe we ought to bring in all the facts before we denounce Canada as being an agent of proliferation. In this case we are an agent of non-proliferation and an agent of economic and social development in countries that desperately need that development.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question for clarification. I understood the minister to say a few minutes ago that Argentina had a small experimental separation unit. I later understood him to say that they do not have a separation unit. If the minister makes a distinction between a large separation unit and an experimental one, may I point out that the explosive device which was produced by India was made from a small experimental unit. A small experimental unit is just as capable of extracting plutonium as a large one, except that it only produces small quantities. That, however, can be accumulated over a period of time.
In view of the statements the minister just made, and in view of the fact that most of what he said today was based on the documents that he will make available to hon. members-the position papers and the actual terms of the contract-is he prepared to give us an opportunity to discuss this at a later date? I received this material at about 10.45 this morning, and the House started at eleven o'clock. I did not have a chance to read these papers. If the minister is basing his whole case on the basis of the documentation with which he is supplying us, as I understand it, we ought to have an opportunity to examine that documentation and then discuss it subsequently at the earliest opportunity.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true I stated that the Republic of Argentina does not have reprocessing facilities of commercial or military significance. I am not an expert on these plants. However, I am advised that the amount of plutonium, provided you had a reactor from which to extract it, that would develop from the plant referred to is not significant and is not a viable danger. That is the distinction to be drawn between the commercial and military significance and the laboratory model, the potential of which I have described as accurately as I can. I have undertaken to consider the possibility of further parliamentary discussion of this question. I repeat that to the House, and do so in good faith.
January 30,1976

The House resumed, from Thursday, January 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-68, an act to amend the Medical Care Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock last evening we were debating the amendments to this act which would limit the annual increase and the per capita costs of insured services under medical care plans. I wish to take a few minutes in an effort to develop background material for the amendments now before us, because of the fact that when the original act came into effect there were many people who said we would be having trouble at about this time. This would now appear to be the case.
Last evening I had reached the point where I referred to an article in the Medical Post, a journal published, rather interestingly, by Maclean-Hunter Limited. I think in a few weeks we will hear more about Maclean-Hunter when we hear how the government wishes to stamp out Reader's Digest and Time magazine. In an editorial written under the date of January 6, 1976, this magazine has some interesting comments which I believe warrant consideration. As I read these excerpts, I should like members to think of the three aspects discussed in this editorial. One relates to the predictions of increased high-cost medical care a number of years ago by very reputable authorities and, second, the fact that there may have been some ulterior motives on the part of the government, first of all when it introduced the plan, and even again now, we might suspect. Third, there is a hint in this editorial of how improvements might be made that would help reduce the cost of medical and health care. I quote as follows from this editorial of January 6, 1976:
All of a sudden the politicians have decided that our sickness care system, which they did much to create, has become too expensive.
Too expensive compared to what?
Apparently most of them have forgotten that Mr. Justice Hall in the Hall Commission report back in 1964 predicted costs would run to 7.04 per cent of gross national product in 1976 and he was working in 1957 constant dollars. At the present time the total cost of all U.S. sickness services is running about 9.0 per cent of that country's GNP. According to figures from the Ontario Ministry of Health the total sickness services in the province is running almost exactly 7.0 per cent of the provincial GNP.
But, of course, the politicians designed an open-ended system, mainly because it looked good to the voters, and decided to operate the entire system through tax revenues, making it look as though the whole service was free. It was not free, of course-it just looked that way because the government undertook all payments and collected all the taxes to pay for it. Thus was the tap of public expectations turned wide open, while the politicians basked in their cleverness.
It did not take long before the deliverers of the service began to realize that having the tap of expectations left on full resulted in a huge demand for service. Eventually the politicians began to realize that once that tap had been turned on full it was extremely difficult to close it off, even a little way. They tried all sorts of maneuvers to turn back the tap without appearing to do so; they accused the doctors of overusing the system and railed against the gross inefficiencies in hospitals
Medical Care
and set civil servants to finding alternatives to the system to reduce costs. But they dared not touch the real problem, that excessive flow of public expectations.
The editorial goes on to say this:
The outcry about accelerating sickness care costs have come mostly from the politicians who are afraid they have come to the bottom of the taxpayer's pocket.
And they are right in that fear.
Yet nobody seems to suggest that perhaps the public look on the present sickness service as so important that it will pay a share of the cost of the service directly-and that the public itself will by this means turn off some of the flow of service expectations which it has been educated to expect.
No politician has broached this because he probably feels his constituents might not like it.
Finally, there is another paragraph which reads:
The idea of having the public pay some of its sickness service directly is probably verboten around the ministry.
It is our opinion that the whole government-financed sickness service has been over-extended and mismanaged since it started. Now financial pressures are forcing governments to look for scapegoats and the sickness service is going to be one of them. It is going to be curtailed whether the taxpayers approve or not simply to bail out a government which has grossly overspent for years.
I draw the attention of hon. members to the three points I raised before I read this editorial. First of all, a person- no less than Mr. Justice Hall who was chairman of the royal commission-anticipated this problem and, second, it is suggested that the government had some ulterior motive in wanting to get votes, by this scheme, back in 1967-68- and one wonders whether this still applies. One begins to wonder whether the government has an ulterior motive now in trying to control the income of physicians by bringing in this bill at the present time. Perhaps more worrisome to some of us is that one wonders whether we will have sprung on us, in the next year or two-or certainly before the next election-some other universal welfare plan that will put us in even deeper trouble.
Perhaps this is the reason the government is trying to cop out of the plan already in effect and is trying to get rid of some of the charges that have been turned over to it in the hope that there will be money left over, somehow, for other plans which will be brought in and which will place another strain on the country. The third thing in this editorial of the Maclean-Hunter Company publication is a hint that probably there is an opportunity yet in this country for Canadians themselves to feel some responsibility for looking after their own health care.
I was encouraged somewhat in the debate yesterday when the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) conducted a very judicious plea as he gave his presentation with respect to this bill. I think my hon. friend and professional colleague from Halton did a good job, riding several horses. He certainly did well on behalf of the medical profession and on behalf of the Canadian Medical Association. I think he did reasonably well on behalf of his government. But I was very pleased to note, as recorded in Hansard of January 29 at page 10450, that he said:
In light of these complexities, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have apparently promised not to impose any more universal programs on the provinces, hopefully, not even on the country.
I hope the hon. member for Halton is correct in that we will not be confronted by this government with more,

January 30, 1976
Medical Care
similar schemes. In reviewing the historical past of this bill, I should like to conclude with a further quotation from someone all government members opposite respect, namely, former prime minister Lester B. Pearson. I shall quote from the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, of November 13, 1975, page 68:185. A submission to the committee at that time contains the following quotation from the statement given by Mr. Pearson:
It is a national responsibility, a federal government responsibility, to ensure that our medical care insurance program is comprehensive, universal, publicly administered and portable. If a certain standard of public medical services is needed and approved by Canadians generally, appropriate fiscal resources have to be brought into play on a national scale-
I underline the word "national".
-in order to make the services available to a national standard in all parts of the country.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, at that time Mr. Pearson felt this was a national responsibility and not something that could be approached in a unilateral and arbitrary way by the federal government alone, as is being done at present.
I should like to move on to other broad areas in this debate. I will touch very lightly on the first one, that is, some of the other effects of the bill before us. This has been dealt with rather adequately by many previous speakers, and I do not wish to take a long time on it. The effect of this bill on the quality of medical care no doubt will be very great, and it is a risk which the people of Canada will be facing. If the federal government puts more of the expenses of medical care on the provincial governments, they will either have to take more money from the people of the provinces or they will have to curtail and limit medical services and other health care services. I think this is a regrettable situation, but I will not take up more time because we have heard about it from several speakers. Incidentally, this is bound to affect the poorer provinces more than the richer provinces, and that is deplorable.
The second area which has been dealt with adequately, both by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), speaking on behalf of the government, and by other speakers on this side, is in connection with the effect this bill may have on physicians' incomes. There are now two pressures on physicians-the anti-inflation measures and the amendments in Bill C-68. This is regrettable, in view of the fact that back in 1971 physicians took the government at its word, and when the Young commission advocated voluntary restraint, that was carried out by the medical profession. They will be the ones to suffer because they tried to co-operate at that time. Enough said about those two situations which I find regrettable.
Now I want to go on to some positive aspects of the legislation before us. I do not want the minister to feel that I am only attacking his policies on health care. Sometimes we hear it said that the opposition parties should always be on the attack. I am not sure that should be so. I think that sometimes positive things come from the government side, and this should be acknowledged. The minister alluded to the fact that there will be some reductions in health care costs by virtue of the seat-belt legislation which is being

implemented across the country gradually, and the reduction in permissible speeds on highways. I dare say he is right to a certain extent, but I would remind him that we are debating a medical care bill, not a health care bill.
If one looks at the medical costs saved by the seat-belt legislation and the reduction in highway speeds, one finds it is true that some reductions may be effected in medical care costs, but they are far greater in the health care field. If a person smashes his head in an accident and lies unconscious in a hospital for six months, the big cost is not the medical cost but the health care hospital cost. If a person has two or three fractured bones and is in hospital for several months, again the medical care cost may be equivalent to four, five or six days of hospitalization, but the hospital stay of three or four months which is required is much more significant. So I think we must not feel too satisfied that by introducing these pieces of legislation we will reduce medical care costs, but we may be largely reducing hospital care costs.
The other matter about which the minister spoke was his effort and the effort of the provincial government to improve our lifestyle as a means of saving health care costs. I think that is commendable, but we should look at one more point in reference to that question. We must begin to think about the concept of an experience rating of our health insurance plans in accordance with our lifestyle. This is not a new concept. We do it now with life insurance and we do it with collision insurance; we also do it through the Workmen's Compensation Board. However, I am not so sure we shouldn't do it with health insurance. People who choose to lead lifestyles that are less than healthy and are conducive to high costs in the health care field perhaps should have to pay their share of that extra cost. That is one thing the minister should consider in the future.
Another possible means of controlling excessive health care costs might be through legal and other mechanisms for providing payment for allied health personnel. We could resort to paramedical professionals, to some extent, who have developed skills that do not require as much training and education as those required by physicians and yet are very essential. The cost of providing such health care assistance is somewhat less. However, the problem is that at present there is no legal mechanism which would permit the practising of those skills or payment for those skills in conjunction with physicians' services. The government should study this matter.
Of course, there are times when hospital facilities can be built more cheaply, and this would reduce health care costs. However, let us revert to the matter of bringing about legal changes in the system. We are fast approaching the state which exists in the U.S.A. where legal actions against physicians and hospitals are increasing at an alarming rate. There is no question that this leads to increased costs of health care, if for no other reason than that physicians and other health care personnel, in order to protect themselves against possible legal action, greatly increase their requests for certain lab work, certain X-ray work and certain consultations. I think we should be looking at ways and means of limiting the number of legal actions and the amounts of these claims to a more reason-
January 30, 1976

able level, thus relieving some of the financial pressure on the health care system.
Another matter that should be considered is that in recent years increasing emphasis has been put on training young physicians in the use of hardware and tjie technology of medicine, rather than in the old skills of history-taking and plain, physical examinations. These have been popular areas to stress in the last few years, but they are expensive and they increase health care costs. Similarly, the situation has been aggravated, I am sure, by the news media which tends to lay emphasis on the heroics of medicine, on heart, kidney or liver transplants as though these were the essence of medicine. I am not trying to deprecate or lower the need for research, both experimental and on humans, but since we are living at a time when costs are to be reduced, we should be careful about the money spent on these heroics in medicine.
Another area to which the minister might like to give consideration is the development of appropriate regulations to discourage high costs. Over the last ten years or so-for example, under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act-the provision regarding X-ray services was such that if you were an out-patient, your X-ray costs were not covered by the insurance scheme, but if you could finagle your physician to admit you to the hospital, your X-ray costs were covered. Not only did the state, or the plan, have to pay for the X-rays in such cases, but it also had to pay for the costs of the stay in hospital.
The same thing occurred with dental care services. For a long time, good dental services with general anaesthesia were being provided in the dentists' offices and the only cost to the plan was for the anaesthesia service. Then the government changed the regulations so that when the patient was admitted to hospital, everything was covered- anaesthesia, hospitalization and, of course, dental services in the hospital. This added further to the expense.
I am pleased to see that the minister is suggesting that he will introduce some low cost medical services into his new plan, and for this I think we must commend the minister, but I caution him in this one particular area. I have had some communication with a provincial minister of health on the topic of nursing homes. I have been approached by a number of my constituents who feel that it is absurd that health care plans should be paying for families to put their elderly relatives into nursing homes. If the children in a family decide that their parents are getting old and need more help, there is an economic advantage to placing them in a nursing home, whereas if the government saw fit to pay perhaps half the price it pays nursing homes on a per diem basis to those same children, they would look after the old folks at home, and everyone would be happier.
I caution the minister that if he is going to put more money into services such as nursing homes, he should be positive and see if we cannot spend that money in a cheaper way which will keep patients out of nursing homes and in their own homes if at all possible.
I am coming close to the end of the points I wish to discuss. There is the matter of perhaps considering transferring some tax points from the federal tax treasury to
Medical Care
provincial treasuries. That would give the provinces some feeling of control over their health expenditures and some assurance of revenue to provide those services.
Another thing the minister might consider under this legislation is removing these arbitrary ceilings he has included and putting them under regulations instead of in the legislation. This would allow some flexibility. We all know how difficult it is and how the government refuses to predict inflation for the future. It must be difficult to plan a rigid percentage at this time which would be appropriate. Surely it would be better to have flexibility built into this.
The government might also consider having a tripartite committee of some sort composed of federal representatives, medical profession representatives, and provincial people who could discuss some of the problems, particularly as they relate to medical care financing for the future.
I wish to conclude with some views on a matter which I think is very important. This relates to something I touched on earlier and something which was touched on in an editorial I read in the Medical Post. This is the matter of patient responsibility for his own health care and his participation as a patient in the provision of his own health care from an economic point of view. I should just like to take a moment to read something further from the report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of the same date as before, November 13, 1975, at page 68:186. This is from the presentation of the Canadian Medical Association to the committee at that time, and I will read from the report:
Public education relative to the prudent use of medical services might help to lower frivolous patient demands for medical services. However, it remains our opinion that unnecessary, frivolous patient demands for medical services and overservicing by physicians would be most effectively controlled by some degree of direct personal responsibility of the patient in the payment for such services.
I will go on to what I think is another very significant quotation on the same subject. This is taken from the Canadian Medical Association Journal of October 18, 1975 at page 792. Dr. Bette Stephenson, now the minister of labour for Ontario and a former president of the Canadian Medical Association, was asked to appear before a subcommittee of the Congress of the United States on health care. They were trying to look into the future of health care plans there, and I quote from the Canadian Medical Association Journal:
Even more important, says Dr. Stephenson, it removes from the patient a feeling of responsibility for his own health. Dr. Stephenson noted that "the most significant advances in the health of our populations will be achieved through increased acceptance of personal responsibility for health maintenance, not through the provision of additional services. By all means protect the American public from catastrophic health care costs, but do not remove the individual patient from the financial aspect of his personal health care. Keep the patient involved."
There are many other areas, in the present concepts our government has, where it is taking away responsibility from the citizens of this country, not only in the health care field but in other fields as well. It seems to be the concept and the philosophy of the government that the more control it can have over the individual, the more effective and better lives the people of Canada will have. This has been proven historically to be wrong over the centuries. Civilizations have gone down to complete failure and doom where this sort of situation has developed. I

January 30, 1976
Medical Care
hope the government will see fit to begin to reverse its stand whereby it takes away all responsibility from individuals.
Just in summary, what I have attempted to do in this debate is discuss the origins and the historical background of Bill C-68 and why, in retrospect, it is completely unnecessary. That could have been predicted years and years ago, and indeed it was predicted. We must beware of further encroachments upon the individuals of this country, whether by more universal health care plans or whatever. Let us beware that there is not some trick in this bill by which the government will introduce something in the next two or three years, or even sooner, which will take away more responsibility from people.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have dealt at some length with a dozen or so ways which I think the Minister of National Health and Welfare should consider appropriate to help reduce both medical care and health care costs.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. S. Victor Railton (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to review this legislation from the standpoint of a doctor. However, I want to make it clear that I support the minister and his legislation.
Bill C-68 is designed to amend the Medical Care Act. It was originally antedated or previewed by the June budget of 1975 introduced by the former minister of finance. In one section of his policy which was for retrenchment he brought out the fact that the government aimed to rewrite the Medical Care Act, or renegotiate the costs and percentages. He laid down ceilings, 13 per cent on increases for
1976-77, IOV2 per cent the following year, and 8'A per cent subsequently. He retained the per capita approach to determine the total contributions to the provinces.
Apparently there is some desire on the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to keep the IOV2 per cent as a figure for the subsequent years, and I think this might be a good idea. No one in the medical profession in this country fights a policy of control very strongly. They recognize the need for prevention of unregulated cost increases in medical care. Somehow both hospitalization and medical care costs will have to be renegotiated, and they might need restructuring. Health delivery care systems may eventually have to evolve, and most doctors are strongly against cuts in national medical research which is given to universities and the Medical Research Council.
In certain countries in Europe, and in the United States, large multinational corporations of the pharmaceutical industry do much original research. Canada enjoys this second hand. These companies also subsidize university and research institutes in those countries.
It is important for Canada to retain her present eminence in research, and it is hoped that the medical research funds will not be cut, but rather that they enjoy the same rate of increase as the hospitals and the medical profession; in other words, according to the present guidelines.
There has been much argument in Canada about the whole health delivery system. The four cornerstones, universality, portability, accessibility, and government

administration are very prominent in our minds. We cannot argue with that a great deal, but in certain ways we do.
The cost of medicare was rising at over 20 per cent annually. It would be irresponsible to allow this to go on. However, the doctors that I know feel that free medical care, irrespective of recipient's income, is one of the weak points of the system. Many people also believe that old age security for everyone cannot be defended.
There is no doubt that health and accident sickness insurance companies were charging in their premiums $1.25 to $1.55 for every dollar of benefit. But cost of administration had risen in the last few years. The government claims it can provide a dollar benefit to hospitals and medical incomes for $1.03 from tax money. This is rather unrealistic to me. This does not take into account any of the expenses required to borrow money or the expense in the civil service for the handling of money. It refers only to the administrative costs of doling it out to the provinces.
Doctors feel, as far as I can make out, that there should be a sliding scale of participatory payment of insurance according to incomes. I agree with that idea. The socialist group feels that a means test is a demeaning manoeuvre. This is not so, in my opinion. The very wealthy would pay a certain premium for the same services and the scale would descend to zero at the poverty line, which would presumably take in a great many of the retired people, invalids, handicapped, and other low income groups. Everybody would be given identical care in doctors' offices and in hospitals.
In Ontario many small hospitals are about to be closed. There is a rumour that the city of Port Colborne may lose its hospital; this would be a shame and I cannot quite believe it.
A sizable percentage of "acute" beds are being closed in every hospital in the province. This is an attempt to reduce the cost of hospital care, and it is quite true that many people are in acute beds who do not need that level of care. It is also true that there is a small percentage of people admitted to hospital and treated surgically as well as medically when these patients are not always in the category of urgent treatment. I think that the type of doctor practising in this manner is not as common as some years ago, but this type of practice did exist. However, I would hope that the provinces will call a halt to the closing of these acute beds at such an alarmingly rapid rate.
Hospital care may be cut to some extent because that was the portion of the cost which was increasing at such a rapid rate. Doctors' incomes have had a low rate of increase for the past several years. It was about 4 per cent in two of the years, 7 per cent plus in another year, and there was no increase in another two years. At the same time one has to remember that there was a windfall increase in doctors' incomes of around 35 per cent to 40 per cent when medicare was institued. This was due to the fact that 90 per cent of the bills were paid instead of 65 per cent to 70 per cent. One cannot forget, however, that the doctor does get paid for only 90 per cent of his potential income under medicare.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare states that doctors will have to regard their raises as related to the
January 30, 1976

year 1971. But more truly would be the years preceding the institution of medicare, because their style of life did rise very quickly since medicare began. All this will have to be accepted. Dr. Grisdale of Calgary, President of the Canadian Medical Association has already appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and indicated acceptance of the guidelines since October, 1975.
One thing that worries doctors in Canada is the role of government in medicine. Our government has a tendency to point to the improving infant mortality and longevity tables as if it were due to medicare. However, these same improvements are present in the United States, where there is no universal medicare. These improvements are really evidence of increased medical and public awareness of the need for better care for pregnancy, good care at childbirth, and the post delivery care of the infant, along with the recent institution of intensive care therapy. Improvement in health in Canada recently stems from the great advance in medicine and surgery following the second world war.
One has to give credit to the provincial governments as well as the federal government for building excellent hospitals in the affluent years of the fifties and sixties. Certainly all these improvements in health have not been due to government interference in the health field, that is, as far as medicare is concerned.
At this time I would deplore attempts to curtail too quickly our present style or system of medical care in hospitals and in doctors' offices. One must realize also that there is a dangerous feeling in some circles that prevention or personal change in living habits will do a great deal to make everyone healthy and almost put the country in such a blessed state that a great reduction in the cost and complexity of medical care can be produced. This, I think, is an impractical dream.
The huge population increases of the past 20 years have been really due to the discoveries in preventive medicine. Starting with such things as prevention of smallpox, plague, typhoid, cholera and other widespread epidemics, and the introduction of antibiotics which have reduced deaths from bacterial infection, to the subject of viruses- which may come under control soon; all these have collectively conspired to lengthen longevity. However, we still do not, and will never have complete control over blood and tissue tumors, natural disasters, road, rail and air accidents, industrial accidents, congenital defects, and defective organ inheritance producing premature mortality. Certainly change of life style, reduction of obesity and other health hints will do something, but will not change much the need for hospital care.
Painful maladies, low back pain, degenerative arthritic joints, causalgic pains have been treated in the past by irregular practitioners, and by everything from quackery to faith healing, yoga, transcendentalism, and acupuncture. Recently there was a scientific breakthrough with the discovery of transdermal electric stimulation. This may be very helpful or even curative. These simply are things which are here and must be mentioned because they do take a lot of medical care and are not amenable to amelioration entirely by "taking thought".
Medical Care
One of the benefits that the voluntary health committee of the House of Commons conferred was to hold a luncheon meeting with Dr. William Ghent of Queen's University, and Dr. Ken Wilson of Ottawa, to discuss the question of traffic accidents. In that committee they showed us that half the mortality, half the morbidity, and half of the cost of traffic accidents could have been prevented. They were working as members of the traffic accident research foundation. This body proved that the total cost to Canada of road accidents is $2 billion annually. The number of lives lost in the province of Ontario is over 1,700 annually.
Prevention is directed to reduction of the number of alcoholic drivers, reduction of the speed limit, and the mandatory use of seat belts. These would be very easy to promote in a big educational campaign on television. I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare is pushing this concept at the present time.
All these things that I have mentioned have helped reduce the amount of sickness and the number of people who die too early, or who are incapacitated by illness. However, there is a belief among some health and welfare officials that we could get along in the future without much medical care if people believed in the precepts of proper personal health direction. I regret to say that this is not at all likely, and I do not think that the present number of hospital beds should be reduced any further.
When this act is passed the provinces of necessity will have reduced their expensive hospital facilities to some extent. By then they can enjoy a long breath as they look forward to the next two years. It would appear that the lOVi per cent would be the bottom of the reduction as allowed for annual increase. This of course will be dictated by the inflationary rate and the new agreements.
When we discuss a health care delivery system we have to admit that our present system has grown without too much planning. It has developed in line with those of all other modern industrial societies. However, we have now a medical profession which is enjoying private practice without its members being salaried government servants as they are in England, Sweden, and to some extent in Germany.
We have built large hospitals with excellent emergency departments and excellent intensive care units. The hospitals have been departmentalized and any urban centre of
20,000	or over has usually had an excellent staff of general practitioners, pediatricians and specialists in all the usual diseases, all well trained and academically certified. Many people wonder why anyone would change this. The only reason of course is to cut costs.
I do not think there is much doubt that in the parts of Canada which have average density of people, medical and hospital care are known to possess the highest quality in the world. When one talks about changing the present system one would have to experiment, and a sudden experiment might be disastrous. At the same time we will have to make some changes in the system. It is quite irresponsible to let total medicare costs absorb more than the 6 per cent or 7 per cent of the gross national product, which they now absorb.

January 30, 1976
Medical Care
I have been in Nigeria where they had one genito-uri-nary surgeon for the whole 20 million people in the north. I have been in India and have seen highly trained specialists congregating in the cities and doing general practice for wealthy people, instead of accepting public health positions at a low salary to bring medical care to the poor.
In Canada our main unserviced areas are on the frontier. Certainly salaried people, doctors, nurses, and technicians, should be provided and are being provided. We are doing our best with aircraft to transport seriously ill victims of sickness or accident to proper centres.
There are very few Canadians who would really accept the second-class services of community centres after having had the high quality medical care which they now enjoy. It is all very well to use a nurse and a nurse-practitioner as front line defence against the surges of applicants for medical care, or to use a surgical technician instead of a doctor to assist in operating rooms. I have gone through all that in my army experience, and in Nigeria. It just is not as good. So I believe that furture lowering of costs can only be done by continuing sensible preventive medicine and pruning frills from hospitals and medical care. Some of these expenditures are due to inertia and laziness. For instance, total laboratory examinations, totally complete X-ray examinations, and total physical examinations sound good, but are merely ways of avoiding taking an interest in each patient, spending the time necessary to dig out a complete and pertinent set of facts about the case history, and doing a fair amount of thinking about the case.
Although we could do much to improve mass health delivery systems, we will never improve on the combination of experience backed by academic qualifications, and the use of brains by the medical practitioner.

I read the speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I am afraid I could be in the House long enough to hear only part of what he said, but I read his speech with great care.
I was also unable to be present in the House when the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) spoke, but I read his speech with great interest. I thought it was a thoughtful and strong speech on the subject. I notice that there was some controversy about the extent to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare listened to the hon. member for Athabasca. I do not know to what extent he was able to listen to the hon. member for Athabasca, but I hope that in this quiet, thoughtful atmosphere he will listen to me.
The hon. member for Athabasca said just about all there is to be said about the bill when he described it as an arbitrary, unilateral act by the federal government. Since I feel that this bill reflects a most arbitrary, unilateral approach to health care and, in a broader sense, to federal-provincial relations, I feel impelled to intervene in this debate, even thought it is 3.30 on a Friday afternoon. But

no matter how eloquent I may be on a Friday afternoon, I doubt if I can express my indignation at this bill.
I hope the minister will not mind my saying that in my various capacities I have been involved in this area longer than he has been. I do not say that with a view to delivering him lectures on how the Department of National Health and Welfare should be run. I say it simply as a preface to my remarks, which arise out of my experience in negotiations connected with health plans.
Although as a provincial premier I was not involved in the negotiation of the hospital plan, I was in politics in those days and followed closely the scope of the plan. I know beyond doubt that the nature and terms of the plan were dictated by the federal government of the day. Some provinces had grave reservations about all aspects of the hospital plan, but the federal government persisted and, eventually, all provinces of Canada were persuaded to participate.

speechtext:
Here we see the government attempting to impose a ceiling unilaterally, not on the cost of medicare in this country but upon the federal government's contribution toward the cost of a program which the federal government itself has insisted that the provinces establish and administer. Madam Speaker, surely treachery is not too harsh a word to use to describe conduct of that kind. There is no other word for it. I must say it is consistent with the behaviour of a government which seems to regard itself as in no way bound by its word.
The minister has offered what he considers to be some concessions. He intends to move amendments which he described as improvements. One of these alleged concessions is that the very arbitrary ceilings on the federal contributions for the years 1976-77 and 1977-78 would be preserved but that from then on a new flexibility will be introduced. The rigid ceiling which was in the previous bill is to be dropped. Let me say that the ceilings for the next two fiscal years are entirely arbitrary. They are not to be related in any way to what will happen, to what the experience of the provinces might be, or to the success or failure the government might have in controlling inflation. The ceilings which remain for the next two years are entirely arbitrary, and the minister cannot justify using those figures or asking parliament to adopt them.
In the second place, far from having made a concession or an improvement in taking out the ceiling for the subsequent fiscal years, the minister is giving himself a blank cheque in those subsequent years. That is what he is asking parliament to do. Much as I would hate to see those set ceilings continue-I would fight them in the next two or subsequent years-I would prefer to see some figures set out in the act than to see the provinces left to the tender mercies of the minister after what he calls consultation with the provinces. I say to him, Madam Speaker, that after the next two years for which there are specific ceilings set out, the government, if it is still in power-and God preserve the people of Canada from such a fate-the minister, or any minister who might be minister of national health and welfare, could arbitrarily impose a ceiling of his own choosing on the contribution the federal government would make to the cost of medicare in this country.
I do not think the hon. gentleman will have much success in persuading anybody on this side of the House, or very many people in the country, that the government will in fact work out an agreement with the provinces as to what those ceilings should be. I am as sure as I am standing here that not one member of any provincial government today believes the Government of Canada will do anything but impose a highly arbitrary ceiling on its contribution following the two years in respect of which ceilings are set out. I say that if parliament passes a bill imposing specific ceilings for the next two years and giving the minister, or the government, the discretion to impose ceilings for subsequent fiscal years, parliament will be participating in a betrayal of the total understanding upon the basis of which this plan was launched a number of years ago.
Medical Care
The minister spoke of incentives. He wants to give the provinces a greater incentive, he said, to control the cost of medicare. As the hon. member for Athabasca pointed out, the provinces already have a very strong incentive to control the cost of hospital care and of the medical program since, in rough terms, they pay 50 per cent of the cost. This, in itself, is a very significant incentive. It is hard enough as it is for many of the provinces to bear the 50 per cent of the cost they are called upon to pay, and they struggle mightily to control the expense of this plan.
If the minister does not yet know, I can tell him it is very difficult for the provinces to control increases in the cost of these programs. Certainly I can speak for my own province. The provincial commission dealing with medicare and the one dealing with hospital care are very tough. If things are anything like they were when I was premier-and I suspect they are-they are constantly at war with many parts of the province in connection with services or improvements which are wanted in one direction or another. The problem is that every body wants as high a standard of service as it suspects anyone else is getting. I just heard the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) say he does not think the number of active beds should be cut down any further. I also heard him say he felt it would be a mistake to bring about any drastic revision of the doctor-patient health delivery system which now exists.
The nature of the plan imposed on the provinces by the government makes its cost very difficult to control. I agree as to the importance of control. I agree also with what the minister had to say about preventive measures which could be helpful. His suggestion about cutting down highway accidents is one which appeals to me. I spoke in the House on this subject the other day and I certainly would support the thrust of his efforts in that direction, together with measures he might propose.
It might well be that health delivery care arrangements could be more efficiently organized, although I would judge from the remarks of doctors to whom I have spoken, and from listening this afternoon to the hon. member for Welland, that there are no great magical possibilities in this area. Granted that there is room for improvement in these delivery systems and that we should try to determine needs, I cannot accept that the federal government, which virtually imposed these plans upon the provinces, should now impose an arbitrary limit on its contribution during the next two fiscal years, trying to arrange things so that, following those two years, it can impose upon the provinces any limit that the minister of health may see fit. That to me, Madam Speaker, is unacceptable.
I do not want to be offensive to the minister or his colleagues, but I have to say that the announcement out of thin air in the budget of the former minister of finance last June, and the subsequent steps the minister of health has taken to implement the announcement, are conduct that I can only describe as shabby and treacherous. I have to say to you, Madam Speaker, that the rules of parliament prevent me from expressing to the minister what I really think of him and his colleagues in this regard. I call upon this House, and upon what I hope are some decent members on the other side of the House, to reject this effort on the part of the minister of health and his colleagues to go
