speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate this afternoon, especially because of the opportunity offered to me to join in the discussion just after the hon. Leader of the Opposition has spoken on the same subject.

I feel it is important that at this point in the debate I seize the opportunity given me to praise the work of the Leader of the Opposition in this difficult period of history for his party. I have admired him especially during the last two weeks because I know he has had some very important decisions to make, and in all of them he has shown a great sense of fairness and justice for all those involved in the forthcoming leadership convention. I am greatly impressed by the way he is performing his present functions.

However, Madam Speaker, I cannot agree with some statements he made today. On the one hand, he said that the federal government had imposed medicare programs on Canada. I do not believe that is correct. On the other hand, he mentioned that in the bill before us, the government is taking unilateral action without giving adequate consideration to the provinces' budgetary plan that must take inflation into account, as all other governments of this country have to do at the present time.
Madam Speaker, when we are talking of consultation, we must not restrict the scope of this term, that is refer to consultation merely in terms of expenditures. When a decision is taken about the number of hospital beds, or about building new hospitals, or else to enlarge existing services, it is quite obvious that all these decisions have an immediate and direct effect on the bill to be paid.
In the context of the present legislation, the federal government is prepared to meet the costs without saying a word about how they are incurred. The provinces have full discretion to plan the extension of their services and the salary scales of health professionals.
Now, Madam Speaker, both factors cannot be excluded from the bill to be paid. Thus, for example, in Ontario in measures announced before the budget speech in June, the salaries shown for health professionnals as well as aids were to be increased by 22.6 per cent for 1976-77, by 20.7 per cent for 1977-78 and by 18.6 per cent for 1978-79. In the same province salary increases of over 50 per cent were granted to nurses on an 18-month period for 1974-75 and they were even prepared to vote another for 1976. Substantial raises were also expected in British Columbia.
It is quite obvious, Madam Speaker, that if all provinces unilaterally establish a fee schedule and decide to plan hospital facilities and to improve medical cares-those are objectives shared by each and every province-all those provinces incur expenses which are certainly desirable but they do so without a second thought for the bill they will have to pay. Those provinces contribute so much to swell the budget expenses that it is impossible even to think about any budget planning in health costs in Canada.

However, Madam Speaker, you know that on October 14 the Prime Minister urged the provinces to better co-ordinate their public outlays because health expenditures are those we will have to reduce in the first place. I cannot think, Madam Speaker, it would be possible to co-ordinate our budgets at both provincial and federal levels unless we have considerably more than an inkling of the amount of the bills we will have to pay within five years.
It is essential, Madam Speaker, that the provinces put their own planning in order, not to prevent them from improving the services they administer to the patients in their own area, but to ensure that the improvement of services will be the same throughout Canada.
It is true that some provinces are in a better financial position. They can put more money in health services than others which unfortunately are financially limited. And those provinces which are financially well-off exercise considerable pressure on those which find it hard to maintain minimum standards.
Bill C-68 does not seek to prevent provinces from upgrading their services or moving within a planning scale. Bill C-68 aims at setting minimum standards within which the federal government will continue to participate in the planning and financing of the existing program upgrading.
Consequently, Madam Speaker, I do not think that the provinces which have additional funds allowing them to keep on upgrading their services will be prevented from doing so in the present situation. The danger and the risk we are now facing is that without this legislation being passed, the financially underprivileged provinces will not be able to catch up with the well endowed provinces which will have made progress while we have lost all control over soaring costs.
Bill C-68 is not then an imperative legislation, it is one which tends to maintain the philosophy the federal government has always advocated and defended since the beginning of the seventies.
You will recall, Madam Speaker, that during those years we had reached an agreement between the 11 government levels to sign the Victoria Charter.
You will also remember, and the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Stanfield) took part in those sittings, that during that conference one province in particular had not given its agreement, mainly on the basis of the coordination of health and social security services in Canada.
Now, it is absolutely striking that today the same province unilaterally supports the objectives of federal coordination and acknowledges that the role of the federal government is to maintain these minimum standards of health and social security services. Therefore, I do not accept, as some members of this House would have us believe by their indignation and their protests, that the provinces are completely unhappy with the health care plan as it is now administered in Canada.
Obviously, there are some parts of the country which are not served adequately. In some regions, there is also a lack of physicians and specialists. It is the responsibility of the province concerned to provide such coordination within
January 30, 1976

the province. It is its responsibility to establish a scale of wages, salaries and allowances which will result in equal health care services for all citizens, wherever they live.
Bill C-68, Madam Speaker, is not designed to keep Canadian citizens from equal access to health, but rather to avoid an over-concentration of health services where the financial basis is wide enough to provinde the luxuries which other areas of the country unfortunatly cannot get in this economic context.
Consequently, far from being in jeopardy, the objectives the government had set itself in the '70s, when it tackled the gigantic task of the internal organization of health services, will be achieved. In fact, Bill C-68 is designed precisely to better guarantee the citizens access to health services in times of inflation. Therefore, Madam Speaker, I cannot agree with claims to the effect that the government is acting unilaterally. On the contrary, the very provinces who are least able to make up for increasing costs are all for Bill C-68.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Not at all, that is simply not true.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
It would never occur, Madam Speaker, to any sensible person, that he should foot the bill without having a say in the decision. Nor would it ever occur to any of the governments in Canada to increase thoses taxes because one of them, whether in Western or Eastern Canada, in central Canada or elsewhere in the country, is adding indirectly to the costs to be borne by the federal government, through its decision to improve its own services over and beyond the national standards.
We are now in a situation where the federal government will have to curtail projects, and programs of extreme importance to the betterment of the living conditions of Canadians, unless it does something about increasing health costs. I feel, Madam Speaker, that Bill C-68 is intended to ensure that the government of Canada maintains its leadership within the minimum standards that must apply throughout the country.
Bill C-68 expresses the federal government's desire to ensure that provincial governments, which want to provide more than minimum standards will seek in their own coffers the money they need to update their medical services. Consequently, this is not unilateral action, but action intended to protect the poorer provinces and allow them to offer the minimum standards within their present medicare services.
The leader of the opposition protests, he has the right and he has to do so. I listened very carefully and I hope that later he will have the opportunity to answer to my questions, but I am personally convinced that the medicare program, as it presently works, was not imposed unilaterally by the federal government. On the contrary, this discussion has been lasting for the last nine years. The first bill was introduced in 1966. The debates lasted more than five months, and though during the 1965 campaign the three main political parties in Canada-the Liberal party, the Progressive Conservative party and the New Democratic Party-all recommended complete medicare, when the vote was taken in the House in 1965 all those parties voted by a margin of 90 per cent for the adoption of the present medicare system. It would be misleading the House to pretend today that the government had imposed
Business of the House
medicare at that time. On the contrary this debate has been going on for nine years. Ever since 1970 there have been many federal-provincial conferences aiming at achieving closer coordination of the health and social security programs. At each stage of the discussion, at each level of decisions, there were press releases expressing the consensus which was beginning to take shape within the different governments of Canada in view of continually improving health care.
However, Madam Speaker, when financial measures aiming at improving the coordination and distribution of funds are adopted there are always government levels or agencies which do not feel free to take advantage of the financial options which may exist within the whole budget. Let us remember that the aims of Bill C-68 are written in the law which was adopted by Parliament in 1965. Therefore it cannot be said that we are dealing with a unilateral measure but on the contrary with a measure which is in keeping with the government's aim to ensure accessibility to the same quality of medical care throughout Canada.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, do all these interruptions come out of my time?
The purpose of this bill is to exercise our right in the Parliament of Canada to amend the British North America Act with respect to matters that are exclusively federal and, in doing so, to increase the quorum for sittings of this House of Commons.
Ever since the year one, namely 1867, section 48 of the British North America Act has read:
The Presence of at least Twenty Members of the House of Commons shall be necessary to constitute a Meeting of the House for the Exercise of its Powers, and for that Purpose the Speaker shall be reckoned as a Member.
I suggest that if any of us were to ask, as I have, ordinary persons what they think the quorum of this place is, from those who do not know you would never receive the answer 20. Some think it is 50 per cent, or 50 per cent plus one, and when you tell them it is not that high they will come down to 100 or even to 50, but those who do not know never come down to 20. They find it difficult to understand when they are told that it is 20 in a House of Commons whose members number 264. They find it difficult to understand that it is only necessary to have 20 members present to carry on the business of this House.
I wonder if hon. members are aware of the reason that figure is there. I suggest it was not just pulled out of a hat. It is the figure that was in the rules of the old parliament of the province of Canada which was in existence from 1841 to 1867. There were in that assembly 130 members, 65 from Upper Canada and 65 from Lower Canada. We have seen again some of the sessions of that House in the Pierre Berton CPR show. I simply say to members that that is where we got the figure 20.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: From Pierre Berton!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Not from Pierre Berton although it would seem that we get a lot of things from him. We got it from a house of 130 members which had a quorum of only 20. When 1867 came along and this
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
House was constituted the original membership was 181. I suppose the Fathers of Confederation thought that if 20 was a sufficient quorum for 130 members it was sufficient for 181 members.
But we are now 264 members, and surely the fact that 20 was sufficient for 181 or 130 does not mean that it is a sufficient quorum for 264 members. As a matter of fact where did that 1841 assembly of the United Province of Canada get the figure 20 as a quorum? It got it from the rules of the assembly of the earlier body which constituted Lower Canada or Quebec by itself. I confess I have not been able to find out how many members were in that body. I hope someone will find out and tell me, but I suspect it was a much smaller number than 130, probably 65, 70, or something like that.
It is all because some time ago in a small body of 60, 70 or so members, 20 was a quorum that the figure 20 has persisted down through the years; now we have 264 members and it is still our quorum under the BNA Act and the Standing Orders of the House. The quorum is still only 20. I do not think that is good enough. I think the public is justified in being concerned that at times the attendance of this House can get so low.
If I seem to be levelling any criticism in saying this I am levelling it at the entire House and at all parties. None of us can throw many stones when we talk about attendance in the House, although I suppose I could put in a word or two to the effect that my attendance record is not bad.

I was hoping I would get applause for that and I thank my hon. friends, especially those opposite.
I know the arguments that will come forward during this debate. Earlier this afternoon I noticed one of the hon. members opposite handing out sheets of paper to four or five members on the government side who usually take part in the talking out process. I asked him where was my speech. He did not give me one, so I have to make my own.

I know one of the main arguments will be that there are other things members of parliament have to do. There are committees, there is work in the office, and there is work back in the constituencies. However, I suggest there never is a time when 244 members have to be out of this House at the same time. That is what is being said when it is argued that the quorum can only be 20 because members have to be somewhere else.
The committee process sometimes becomes almost impossible, but we never have more than five committees meeting at the same time. That would account for 100 members, but our membership is 264 and I submit that

these arguments that we cannot be here because of the requirement to be other places does not really stand up.
It is argued of course that all the debates are not exactly interesting. I suppose that is an argument which could be made right now; why stay in the House to listen to me speak? This is the main thing we are elected to do. We are elected to be members of parliament and to participate in the democratic process here on the floor of the House of Commons. We have to do a lot of other things, too, and we do them.
This is a full time job. I do not think any of these arguments excuse us from having a much better attendance in this House than we have a good deal of the time. We are here at two o'clock. This place is almost full and the press gallery is full, but a little later there are very few members here except the Friday afternoon faithfuls who are always here, and we still have one faithful in the press gallery.
Someone will point out that I have introduced this bill quite a number of times. That is true. I have not counted the number of times but it is probably 10, 15 or 20, and I have not yet succeeded. I think I shall win my point very soon. I may not win it by getting this bill passed or by having the quorum increased, but I think I shall win my point that there should be better attendance in the House. Do you know what will do it? Television.
If we get the television cameras in here and the people back home start to say, "I was watching the House of Commons the other day-where were you because I did not see you?"-this will have its effect. I hope that day is not far off. There is a motion on the order paper having to do with this and the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has spent a good deal of time on it. I do not think this is far down the line. So, as I say I hope that day will soon come and we will have better attendance in the House because the people will be watching us and expressing to us the view that we ought to be here.
I know one argument that will be raised against increasing the quorum to 50, which is what my bill proposes to do, and which I believe is consistent with 20 prior to 1841 and 20 between 1841 and 1867, will be that because of one rule, namely, that when the House is found to be short of a quorum it must adjourn for the day, this would put us in some difficulty.
One of my colleagues whom I shall not name said to me when he heard what I was going to do at four o'clock, "What do you want, Stanley; do you want the House to adjourn every day?" I want to say that frankly I look forward to next Friday when I am sure that group over there will increase from five to eight. They must not overdo it!
My hon. friend knows from the friendship between us and the very high regard that I have for him that I make those remarks in friendship, and I make them knowing that there is perhaps no one more concerned about the proper workings of this House and its committees than is the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I think that is acknowledged. However, there are some who are equally concerned, and I suppose there are some who do not really care, but the majority of us care rather strongly about how this House looks.
However, you know, Madam Speaker, there is a lot more to parliament than how it looks. There is a lot more to being a member of parliament than appearing in the Chamber, although I would have to say that this Chamber is the focal point of parliamentary life.
I believe the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) touched on something that was quite important a few moments ago. He spoke about the quorum in the British House of Commons. The membership in that House is over 600, and yet their quorum is only 40.
The British House of Commons is held up as the model for the operation of this House of Commons. One of the things that struck me when I first visited it was the difference in the size of the chambers. Their chamber is small and compressed. But the debates I have heard there on six or seven occasions had a spontaneity about them

and an element of true debate which is not present in this House in the sense of the interruptions, the back and forth throwing of comments, and the exposure in a graphic way of the two sides of the coin, and in some cases three sides of the coin, because we have to remember that we have a minority party of some significance in the House, at least in their estimation of some significance.
I think we made a mistake in some respects in terms of the workings of this House when some time ago we increased the membership of the House. I think we could have considered decreasing the size of this House physically, the removal of the benches to provide a real debating chamber, which there is in fact at Westminster. There are some nights when it is dull there. However, I remember the last time I was there in November of 1974, and they were debating emergency legislation arising out of the difficulties they were having with IRA activities in London and in the surrounding communities. The day I was there a bomb went off in Piccadilly as I was walking through Piccadilly.

I disclaim any responsibility for that happening, but nonetheless I was there, and the headlines of the papers in London were dramatising that situation. The House of Commons was under guard on that occasion. Even with the pass given to parliamentary visitors one could not go from one door to another within the building without being stopped. It was a very dramatic situation. The House was not full for the question period, only half full.
As the debate wore on through the night there were fewer members on that occasion of great emotion in the British House of Commons than there were here throughout the whole of the all-night debate we had with respect to the rail stoppage some time ago. Yet the quality of that debate in terms of the issues being discussed was one of the high points in my life in terms of listening to the utterances of public men in the forum to which they were elected.
When we are dealing with this matter we must be sure we are not dealing with it only in terms of cosmetics. Members of the public have come to me saying that the House is empty and that there should be better attendance. I think the House would be full if there were always the drama of the question period or an emergency situation of some kind, but our life is not like that, and our House of Commons is a reasonable reflection of our life in this country. While I sympathize with the objectives of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I do not think this is quite the way this should be done. It is true that the life of a member of parliament is different now than it was in 1867 when this parliament started, or during the existence of the parliament of Upper Canada when the quorum was higher.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
My hon. friend referred to Upper Canada in the course of his remarks. There has been a basic change in our community, our society, and our way of life. We have much faster communication than there was at that time in terms of telephone, mail-sometimes-and in terms of the ease of people moving back and forth across the country. What has happened is that there is a burden placed upon a member of parliament-and I do not use that word in its usual sense-such as was never a burden in those days and which, by the way, is not the burden of a member of parliament in the United Kingdom today, and that is the intensity of the day to day constituency work of a member of parliament.
I do not have to quote the numbers of letters, requests, complaints, suggestions, and other things which have to be acknowledged and dealt with by a member of parliament. The office work of a member of parliament is a very important part of his representative capacity.
The hon. member mentioned House committees. There are a tremendous number of them. I suggest that perhaps we might think they are too large, but as our society changes and becomes more complex we will be working more and more in House committees.
I dare say our speeches are too long. I think they are repetitive. I think hon. members on the government side are from time to time too silent-and I do not necessarily mean to criticize the government, although that would be a delightful thing from the point of view of the opposition- in terms of exposing the two or three sides of every issue in a way which does not happen at this time.
If there were something interesting, engaging or absorbing in terms of a particular member of parliament and his responsibilities for his constituency, I dare say that member of parliament would be here for that occasion, but I think it can reasonably be argued that if the issue could be handled with greater knowledge by other members of parliament because they live with a particular problem, then those not directly involved ought not to have to sit in the House. If they do sit in the House they may be neglecting another very important part of their responsibility in representing 125,000 or so Canadians. Speaking candidly, I think we have lost a bit of spontaneity in debates because people tend to read speeches, and we tend to speak to each other-

Madam Speaker, my time is getting rather short, but let me say that I think everyone in this House appreciates the intentions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not think there is any doubt about that, but if all of us and those who are observers of this House of Commons would think about it for just a moment-and certainly all hon. members have thought about it-there are many things in terms of some of the matters I have mentioned which might achieve what the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) has urged for parliament, that is, to make parliament live a bit more than it does.
I think it is important as well that while we have shortened the time for communication-we have electronic devices to help us, computers that solve problems in a shorter span and we can produce things more quickly-we should note that the average member of parliament still just does not have enough time. I think all of us, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, want to improve this House of Commons realistically for the benefit of members on all sides of the House.
I hope I will be forgiven if I say I am particularly interested at this point in improving the rules and other amenities of this House for members of the opposition. I think that is important to the parliamentary process, but the procedure that the hon. member has proposed is not going to do that for members of parliament in their representative capacity. I want to thank all hon. members for their interest this afternoon, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is grateful as well.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to, and I will retain my great personal respect for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), not only because of my admiration for him personally as well as with respect to his role as one of the leading members of the House of Commons but also because he is renowned as one of less than a handful or fewer members of the House who are experts in parliamentary procedure.
I am going to do everything I can to make a distinction between the hon. member personally and my feelings about Bill C-267, which I find utterly without merit and which completely dissatisfies me.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proposes that we increase the quorum from 20 members of parliament to 50. The suggestion seems to me to be something less than meritorious. It seeks not only to worsen an already unsatisfactory situation in this House but goes even further, and suggests in effect that we willingly take this House back to nineteenth century Britain when the British parliament was organized to meet the convenience of a small group of titled lords and not very busy ministers.
The hon. member knows very well indeed that it is the governing party, the majority-in this parliament the Liberal party-which is traditionally bound to provide sufficient members to meet the quorum of 20. Not only do we do that but as the governing party we provide approximately 70 members from this side as ministers, parliamentary secretaries, Speaker and Deputy Speakers, committee chairmen, whip, deputy whips and so on. On top of that work load and time load, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre now suggests that we add still further to the problem by having to meet a quorum of 50 rather than 20 members.
Hon. members should look around the Chamber. There are at least two Liberal ministers here and there are 25 or perhaps 30 members of the Liberal party here. As is the case today, and is the case every day of every week in this House, it is this party that provides the quorum, not the NDP, not the Conservatives, and not the Social Credit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had simply suggested in his bill that he wanted to amend the British America Act and the standing rules of the House to provide there would be all party responsibility for this quorum and every party would contribute to the time factor by having its members sitting tied to their desks, I might have found some sympathy for him.
I certainly do not find any sympathy for the bill the way it stands. It would simply see more Liberals tied at their desks in this House while members of his own party and other opposition parties rush across the country suggesting to citizens that the government is not getting its legislation through, that we are not doing our job, that parliament is not working. It is no bloody wonder! It is because we are tied to our desks here while at the same time no similar obligation rests on members of the opposition.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
I would suggest to the hon. member that he take his idea back to his caucus, then go to the Conservative caucus and the Social Credit caucus and tell them that they are going to supply the quorum. I would be delighted if that happened. I do not think they would buy the idea.
Other members have referred to the British House of Commons. The quorum there is 40 out of 635 members. That is 6 per cent of the membership. Our quorum is 20 out of 264-8 per cent. The hon. member now proposes we go to a quorum of 20 per cent or 50 members. What for, Madam Speaker? To make us look better for the media? The media regularly report to the country at large that the House is empty but they never bother to say that there are scores and scores of members in their offices or in departmental offices, or seeing constituents, or working on legislation, or working on committees.
I am not going to suggest that we add 30 more Liberal members of this House-the governing party-simply to satisfy someone who says it looks better, when he does not bother to explain that every member of the House from every party has too heavy a work load already. There is no rationale to this House sitting the number of hours it does. There is no rationale to members sitting here day and night.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: I know my next remark can be interpreted personally by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I do not mean it that way, I mean it with the greatest respect; but some of us do have families and I am getting a little fed up watching the effects on my children of not having a father 12 or 14 hours a day.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I want to remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre of something. He and I, with others on the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, went to London to study the system at Westminster. We were very impressed with their efficiency because in two or three days they can get legislation through the system whereas it takes us two or three weeks, or months!
We wound up at a meeting where we talked to a very important person in the labour party. I am not going to mention his name. We were from all parties in Canada and I do not want to embarrass anybody by mentioning his name, but he was very senior in ranking. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows who I am talking about. We admired the system in Britain and we said, "You are so efficient, but how do you deal with the third party, the minor parties? How do you make sure they can participate in the system?" It was the very senior Labour party man who responded, and I quote him exactly, "We treat them with the contempt they deserve". We do not treat the smaller parties in this House with that contempt, Madam Speaker.
Look at the committee system here. If there were any rationale to the quorum being proposed by Bill C-267, why is it that in the committee system virtually every committee with which I am familiar has already organized matters so that no vote will be taken in the absence of one of the
January 30, 1976

minor parties? We give them that courtesy. What do we get in return? A demand that 50 Liberal members sit here listening to opposition members drone on for hours on end.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: As you are doing now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

If that comment came from the Conservative benches I want to make it very clear that logic and history say we are going to change sides, and some day the people on the Conservative side are going to form the government of this country. I do not think they are any more anxious to put up with this procedural flim-flam than I am or anybody else on this side.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: I hear silence from the Conservatives.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

I want to point out some of the difficulties. We all talk about the UK system, about the mother of parliaments, but I should like to point out a couple of defects.
I am fed up seeing 30 ministers of the Crown sit here every day for an hour and a half when they do not have to be here, when three quarters of them are not asked any questions whatsoever, and the balance from time to time cannot believe the lack of organization in the questions they are asked. The administrative and executive time of the governing party is tied up partly on the front benches. In the United Kingdom there is a roster system and the men and women of parliament are out doing their jobs, not sitting twiddling their thumbs and waiting to answer questions that never come.
I am fed up seeing the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) put in the same position every day. In the U.K. the Prime Minister goes before the House of Commons for question period maybe every two weeks, or on special occasions. In addition, the questions addressed to the Prime Minister of the U.K. are written in advance, provided to him in advance; hence he has the opportunity to answer them properly. The problem here is that we are continually agreeing to allow the question period to be completely the prerogative of the opposition parties; the cost is that we are tying up talent and all sorts of qualified people who are not needed for the theatre, so to speak.

speechtext: The hon. member is making a modest speech.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

I cannot find any merit at all in this bill. It seems to have something to do with cosmetic effects for the press and news media. Is it felt that it will look better in the press if we fill the House with more members? If that is the theory, I do not want to stay here tied to a desk for the benefit of the news media. That is not my role in
House of Commons
life. Perhaps we should change the law, or the constitution, and secure better attendance in the press gallery.
I find no merit in this bill, with one exception. Obviously it has made one backbencher damned annoyed. I will put it this ways. I have been here only three years, and I am sure members far senior to me are laughing because they recognize the frustration of backbenchers with procedures of the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Give up.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

To those who are ready to give up I say I am not yet ready to give up. This question will resolve itself in one of two ways. Either we are going to satisfy the Canadian people that we are serious and here to do our best to meet the problems of this country, or we will continue to operate some sort of play-pen in which half a dozen, or a dozen, or some small number enjoy the use of particular procedures available, and carry on to the detriment of getting legislation through the mill.
If it remains a playpen, those on my side will face one of two courses of action. Either we will get the opposition party, or opposition parties, to agree to reform the rules, soon, soon, soon-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: -or I, for one, will stop being gentlemanly about it, go to the backbenchers of my party and plead to the best of my ability that we use the government majority and steamroller through reforms, and do away with the archaic, stupid tactics which are constantly being used in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: That is a truly Liberal speech.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

No one can deny the urgent need for the reform of the rules of this House. There are several areas of reform with which I shall deal as I proceed. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is taking the wrong approach, and that is only one reason why I oppose this bill.
That reform of the rules is necessary is self-evident; but I am convinced that the kind of piecemeal approach which this bill represents will only add to the continuation of our archaic rules and procedures. Changes must come, but in an orderly and systematic fashion.

It is my hope, indeed, that if no agreement in the near future can be reached among the parties represented in this House-and I mean in the very near future-the government will have the guts to bring before the House a package of reforms and put them through, so that we can operate in the twentieth century, not in the nineteenth century.
As my colleague said, our present rules might have been all right in 1867, in Great Britain; perhaps they were suitable to a gentleman's debating society, or suitable for members who came from the landed gentry of a compact nation. But even in 1867 they were not applicable to Canada, I suggest; certainly they are not applicable to us now.
This is a large country geographically and, as the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has said, members of this House have many duties to perform besides sitting in this House. We have other responsibilities.
I am glad the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore mentioned family responsibilities, because I see no reason why being elected to this parliament should mean that we should have to abandon our families, let our children grow up without their fathers and, as fathers or mothers, miss the developing years of our children's lives. It is not right, it is not fair, and is not part of our service to this nation.

May I quote briefly from Appendix "C" of the report of the Committee on Procedure and Organization dated November 20, 1975. Referring to procedural reform, the committee asks: "How does the Commons use its time?" The answer is as follows:
In the present session of parliament-up to the summer adjournment-the greatest proportion of time of the House of Commons was taken by matters other than government business. About 45 per cent was taken by question period, private members' hours, questions of privilege, adjournment debates and so on. Somewhat less than 40 per cent of the Commons' time was taken by consideration of government bills. Tne remaining 15 or so per cent of the time was taken by consideration of other government motions or on the Business of Supply, the approval of expenditures, (which takes place on days that are colloquially, but not completely accurately, called "opposition days").

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I do not know why it should make the two members of the NDP present in the House uncomfortable to hear how the time of the House has been wasted. But, if it does, I shall cease quoting from the document before me.
If we are to amend the British North America Act, and amend the quorum, we must introduce some other amendments as well. We must eliminate the practice of sitting here half the night three or four days a week. There is no need for it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
We must shorten the length of speeches and stop members from speaking for hours and hours on any particular bill or motion. There is no reason why members other than ministers or party leaders should speak more than 15 minutes on any topic. As far as I am concerned, 40-minute speeches on the part of other members of the House are unnecessary.
We must also place limits on the time available for the debate on any bill, and allow members to make arrangements whereby they can make regular and sensible visits to their constituencies. Also, we must assign to the minority parties in this House time limits proportional to their representation in this House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: The purpose of the bill is very, very clear; it concerns the quorum in the House of Commons. The hon. member talks about changes to the procedures of the House. This is not included in the bill today. The bill clearly concerns the quorum in the House of Commons. The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I thought I was trying to explain why I could not support the bill, but I shall not argue with your decision.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Take your punishment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
A little punishment would not hurt you. We got it on Bill C-69 which the NDP held up for a week, and the hon. member who orchestrated it all was not even here for the vote.
As to the quorum which has been suggested, would it be required that each party should provide members of that quorum in proportion to its strength in the House, or would that responsibility be foisted mainly on members who sit on the government side, placing more work and

more pressure on us in addition to our other duties in committees and elsewhere?
Will it mean, also, that in increasing the quorum in the House we should also increase the number of members required to stand up to demand a recorded vote so that the NDP, for instance, could not on any given day chain five of their members to the Chamber and then pop up and down every whip-stitch to require recorded votes in the House?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he, along with that, say that when someone says no to a request to move a motion under Standing Order 43 he should stand up?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM

Sure. I would be most happy to stand up.
I intend to end my speech, now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: With all those notes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: What is being put forward here today is not reform, it is a posture, and it is an excellent example of the waste of the time of the House to which I have been referring.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to say just a few words about Bill C-257. First, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for presenting this bill.
No, I do not congratulate him directly because of the bill, but I am glad that he has given us the opportunity in the House to say something about the business of the House because we often hear things about attendance in the House which are not justified. The mover of the bill uses a comparison to ask for a quorum of 50. He compares the present situation with a past period, when there was an Upper and a Lower Canada. To be logical in his comparison, he should also compare the number of committees now and at that time. There may be twice as many members now, but there are now three times as many commitees. Indeed, 26 committees sit at the same time as the House. I heard someone say: We shall force representatives of all parties to take part in the quorum in the House. I was wondering how a party like ours could meet this requirement when seven, eight or nine committees sit on the same day. Madam Speaker, this comparison is impossible to make. It is simply illogical.
Regulations concerning the business of the House have now changed, and if we require the same quorum as in the past, it is because a greater number of members must work outside the House. I am glad to have this opportunity to reply to the people, since this will be read by the public. If we truly want to require a quorum when the House is fully capable of sitting, the quorum should also be required between two and three o'clock during the question period. I believe that this is the quorum that we could require, increase, double or triple. Apart from that, apart from the question period, as was said earlier, hon. members leave and the House becomes empty. How many times will we hear this? What the people do not know is that the House becomes empty because two thirds of the members have to sit on their committee and work there the rest of the
House of Commons
afternoon and often in the evening. If we want to come back to quorum of 50, we shall have to disband committees, to stop working in committee and do all the work in the House. Then it would be logical. But if we continue working in committee, I believe that it is illogical to require a quorum in the House. I do not have the time to speak about our work in general, others have done so in my place, but I still wish to congratulate the hon. member for giving another opportunity to the population to obtain some information. Those who read Hansard will learn something about the business of the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are only a couple of minutes left, but I should like nevertheless to make some observations.
It is significant that the proposer of this bill should come from the one party which, from my nine years' experience in the House, has drawn attention to the lack of a quorum. A little game is played frequently. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) is particularly expert at it. He looks around the House. If he thinks there are not enough people here he persuades his colleagues to go behind the curtain. He alone of that party is in the House, and there is a quorum called. It is a nice little game. The last time it was played was in 1974 when the question of the salaries of members was raised.
The hon. member who raises this point today talks in a bland way about the need to improve parliament although he knows himself that if this bill were accepted, with its one change, it would be totally unworkable and would make this place look ridiculous. He knows himself, by his own admission, that a number of other changes would have to go with it. He suggested, for example, not adjourning the House when a quorum fails. Why? I suggest something else should go with it. When a quorum fails Mr. Speaker should look at any party which has fewer than ten of its members in the House and not recognize any of them for the next week in question period. Maybe that would have an interesting effect.
What should we do with regard to opposition days, Madam Speaker? I suggest to my colleagues that there is no reason why they should make up the quorum when the opposition makes thundering charges against the government, and a few moments later there is nobody from the NDP party sitting in the House while it is considering their opposition motion. I think the rest of us should not be faced with the obligation of the quorum at all. If those who want to present a charge against the government are not sufficiently interested to make up the quorum themselves I see no reason why we on this side should make it for them.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE HOUSE OF COMMONS QUORUM
speechtext:
There are many games we can play, Madam Speaker, if we choose to do it, if we choose to be irresponsible, if we choose to be like the colleague of the hon. member who moved this bill today, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). This, as we all recognize, does not bring credit on parliament. This one bill, with its single proposal, would be unworkable and would bring discredit on this House. It would have to be part of a package, a
